whatItDoes: Calculates the Compound Annual Growth Rate of an investment. Given a beginning value, an ending value, and the number of years, it returns the constant annual growth rate that would produce the final value.
whyItExists: Simple return figures don't capture how long an investment grew. CAGR smooths that fluctuation into one annual rate, so different investments and holding periods can be compared apples-to-apples.
whoShouldUse: Investors, portfolio managers, and analysts measuring fund or stock performance across multi-year periods.
useCases: Normalize returns of investments held for different durations
Compare mutual funds and stocks that have been held different lengths of time
Report one growth rate for a whole holding period
Decide between assets by their annualized growth rather than total gain
Measure business revenue or profit growth over several years
Benchmark a fund's return against an index like the S&P 500
instructions: Enter the value you started with (beginning value)
Enter the current or final value

Compare several investments using their CAGR figures

examples: $10,000 to $13,000 in 4 years → CAGR ≈ 6.8%, even though the total gain was 30%
bestPractices: Use CAGR for comparisons, not as a prediction of the future
Include all fees exactly as they affect the value

commonMistakes: Treating a single year's gain as a multi-year rate
Forgetting to include brokerage fees and dividends in beginning/end values
Comparing CAGRs of periods of very different length
Entering the rate as a fraction of a whole year
Using CAGR to forecast — it describes past growth, not future returns
faq: Does this tool support multiple currencies? — Yes, select your currency from the dropdown. All calculations run locally in your browser.
What does CAGR mean? — The Compound Annual Growth Rate: the constant annual rate that grows the beginning value to the end value.
Is it the same as an average return? — No, it accounts for compounding and flattens volatility.
Can CAGR be negative? — Yes, if the ending value is below the beginning value.
Is my data stored? — No, everything runs in your browser.
Does CAGR account for risk? — No, it is a single growth rate; two investments with the same CAGR can have very different risk profiles.
Should I use CAGR or total return? — Use total return to see the headline gain, and CAGR to compare across different holding periods.
assumptions: Generic CAGR calculation; no country-specific assumptions.
